transcript.content: Hi, welcome in—I'm Dr. [Name]. What brings you in to see me today?

Well… thank you for seeing me, Doctor. I’m not trying to make a fuss, and I hope this doesn’t sound unreasonable, but there’s been an ongoing situation in my apartment building.

For months now, the property manager and—well, certain people in the building—seem to be pressuring me to leave. It’s not one big thing, exactly. It’s misdelivered mail, noises in the walls that happen at very particular times, and little comments from neighbors that line up too neatly. They give explanations, paperwork, that sort of thing, but it doesn’t change the pattern I’m seeing. I just thought I should talk to someone about it and make sure I’m handling it appropriately.
How long have you been noticing these signs that people in the building are trying to get you to leave—days, weeks, or longer?

It’s been… longer than days or weeks. I’d say about 11 months now, since not long after I moved into the new apartment. I know that’s a long time to be noticing things, and I don’t want to overstate it, but that’s the best estimate I can give.
Have you ever heard voices or sounds, or seen things, that other people around you didn't seem to notice or hear?

No, I don’t think so. I mean, I hear the building noises, but they’re real noises—pipes, walls, people moving around, that sort of thing. I haven’t, uh, seen things that weren’t there or heard voices talking to me, if that’s what you mean. At least not that I’m aware of.

Over the past 11 months, have you also noticed any periods of unusually elevated mood, increased energy, or decreased need for sleep, or conversely, periods of deep sadness, low energy, or loss of interest in things you used to enjoy?

I don’t think so, Doctor. I mean, this whole situation has been stressful, so I suppose I’ve had some off days, but I wouldn’t say I’ve had those big mood swings you’re describing. I haven’t felt unusually energized or like I didn’t need sleep in any dramatic way, and I don’t think I’ve been deeply depressed either. At least… not in a way that seems out of proportion. Does that make sense?

Before this situation with your apartment building started, would you say you've generally had a long-standing pattern of being suspicious or distrustful of other people's motives, even in other areas of your life?

I’m not sure I’d put it that way, Doctor. I mean, I’ve always tried to be careful and… practical about people’s motives, especially in work settings, but I don’t think I went around assuming the worst of everyone.

Before the apartment situation, I wouldn’t have described myself as especially suspicious. Maybe a bit cautious, but not… not distrustful as a pattern, if that’s the distinction you’re making. Does that answer it the right way?

Over these past 11 months, has this concern affected your ability to work, maintain relationships, or take care of your daily responsibilities, or have you been able to keep functioning normally in those areas aside from this specific worry?

I think, overall, I’ve kept up with things pretty well… at least when I’m not caught up in the apartment issue itself.

I still manage my finances, cook for myself, keep my appointments, that sort of thing. And if I’m talking about consulting work or painting, I can be organized and follow the conversation normally. So I wouldn’t want you to think I’ve just fallen apart, because I really don’t think that’s the case. Does that answer what you’re asking?

final_diagnosis.reason: Patient presents with a fixed, non-bizarre delusional belief (that the property manager and neighbors are conspiring to force her out of her apartment) lasting approximately 11 months, well beyond the 1-month threshold required for delusional disorder. There are no hallucinations, no disorganized speech, and no negative symptoms suggestive of schizophrenia. Mood episode criteria for a manic, depressive, or mixed episode are explicitly denied, ruling out a primary mood disorder with psychotic features. Functioning outside the specific delusional theme remains largely intact (she manages finances, cooking, appointments, and consulting/painting work), which is characteristic of delusional disorder rather than schizophrenia, where functional decline is more pervasive. There is no premorbid history of pervasive suspiciousness that would suggest paranoid personality disorder predating the delusion. The circumscribed nature of the belief system, absence of hallucinations, preserved functioning, and duration >1 month support a diagnosis of Delusional Disorder, Persecutory Type (F22).
